title: Weight Converter
description: Pour a kilogram of salt out as a thousand grams, gather grams back into kilograms, and add and subtract weights in columns.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Change kilograms into grams and grams into kilograms by seeing a kilogram bag break into a thousand grams and gather back, change a weight in kilograms and grams, and add and subtract weights in columns with a carry or a borrow.
writeup.look: A kitchen scale with a kilogram dial and a gram dial, a real bag of salt that pours out a thousand gram marks inside a vermilion ring, a Given tag, an Answer tag, a column board with a kilograms column and a grams column, and two shopping baskets.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Weight Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many conversions or sums have been worked. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A kitchen scale stands at the left, 300 across at x 90, y 220, with a round kilogram dial and a round gram dial side by side on its face, each 110 across, and a real white paper bag of salt labelled 1 kg on its pan. Beside it the kilogram stepper at x 90, y 540 (300 by 60) sets from 1 to 20 kilograms, and the grams stepper under it at x 90, y 610 (300 by 60) adds a number of grams for a weight in kilograms and grams. The Pour and Gather buttons stand at x 90, y 690 and x 250, y 690, each 150 by 56 and labelled in words. When Pour is pressed each kilogram bag opens and pours out its thousand gram marks, drawn as ten small paper bags of 100 g, each cut into ten tens, into a tray at x 420, y 230 (560 by 300) inside a vermilion ring labelled Unit fact, 1 kg = 1000 g. Gather runs it backwards, the gram marks flowing back into kilogram bags, one bag for every thousand, with a leftover of fewer than a thousand staying on the tray as grams. A deep blue Given tag at x 420, y 560 (260 by 60) names the weight the question gives, a green Answer tag at x 700, y 560 (260 by 60) names the weight the working reaches, and an amber Second tag at x 560, y 640 (240 by 56) holds the grams added on, each with its unit beside its number. On the fourth phase the column board replaces the tray: a board 520 by 280 at x 420, y 220 with two columns, kilograms and grams, headed in words, the first weight in the top row, the second weight one row under it, a short level line under them and the answer row below, with a small carried one drawn above the kilograms column and a borrowed kilogram broken into a thousand grams above the grams column. The two shopping baskets stand at x 960 and x 1060, y 220, each a basket of fruit in natural colours about 90 across, and a Basket button under each sets it on the scale. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the converted weight, the sum or the difference into the answer slot. On the first phase the answer slot asks for grams, and on the second for kilograms. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate, labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag, labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from sit inside a vermilion ring, labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag, labelled Second or Left. Every ruler mark, scale mark and plain edge is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a measure is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The scale shows the last weight in both units, the bag poured out into its grams inside the vermilion ring, and the column board with its carry or borrow.

writeup.delight: On the first phase, the moment Pour is pressed, the bag of salt tips and the grams run out in ten small bags that each split into ten tens, inside the vermilion ring, and the kilogram dial turns to zero while the gram dial climbs. On the fourth phase a borrowed kilogram snaps into a thousand gram marks that slide across into the grams column.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase the kitchen scale holds a closed bag of salt and the kilogram stepper is set, with a vermilion ring waiting beside it. On the second a heap of gram marks lies on the scale, the Gather button is lit, and empty kilogram bags wait beside it. On the third the scale reads a weight in kilograms and grams, a Given tag names it, and an empty amber Second tag waits. On the fourth the column board is up with two weights written one under the other and two baskets of fruit beside it. One thing moves, once: the Pour button, or the first column on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any whole number of kilograms from one to twenty on the pan, the Pour and Gather buttons, a weight in kilograms and grams, the column board and the two baskets. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on a bag of salt, a bicycle, a parcel, a desk, a school backpack, a sack of flour and two baskets of fruit, changing both ways, kilograms and grams together, a zero in the grams, a borrowed kilogram, and which basket weighs more.
voiceLines: A kitchen scale and a bag of salt. Let us see what is inside a kilogram.
One kilogram pours out a thousand grams. How many grams does this weight pour out?
Every thousand grams make one kilogram. How many kilograms are in this heap?
Change the kilograms first. Then add the grams that are left. What is the weight in grams?
Work the grams first. Do the grams reach a thousand, or are there too few? Then the kilograms.
A new weight on the scale. Which unit does it start in?
Free play. Pour, gather and add any weights you like.
Look at the grams again. How many thousands are there? Then the grams that are left.
You changed kilograms and grams both ways, and you worked the columns grams first.

observations.why: every kilogram bag holds one thousand grams, so each bag adds another thousand.
observations.soWhat: kilograms change into grams by multiplying by one thousand.
observations.observe: One kilogram bag poured out the same number of gram marks every time, and three bags poured out three times as many.

observations.why: a bag takes exactly one thousand grams, and fewer than a thousand cannot fill a bag.
observations.soWhat: grams change into kilograms by dividing by one thousand.
observations.observe: Gather made one kilogram bag for every thousand gram marks, and what was left stayed as grams.

observations.why: the kilograms and the grams are two parts of one weight, and the kilograms are changed first.
observations.soWhat: a weight in kilograms and grams is changed to grams by changing the kilograms and adding the grams.
observations.observe: A weight in kilograms and grams came out as the kilograms' thousands with the grams added on the end.

observations.why: the grams can reach a thousand and make a kilogram, so the kilograms column needs to know.
observations.soWhat: weights are added and subtracted in columns, the grams first, with a carry or a borrow when the column needs it.
observations.observe: The grams column was worked before the kilograms column, and a thousand grams carried over as a kilogram.

model.answerGate: Every question is gated by its act (user mode, after a real touch): P1 Open (the hand opens each 1 kg bag); P2 Gather (the hand fills a 1 kg bag for every 1,000 g); P3 the right one of Carry and Borrow (shown together; the other gets a nudge and costs no try); P4 a tap on each item (its weight goes into the columns). No question is ungated.

ladder: Count 1,000 g for every bag on the scale.
Add 1,000 g for the first bag and 1,000 g for the second.
items.win: Yes, 2 kg is 2,000 g: each kilogram is 1,000 g.

ladder: Four opened bags make four thousands of grams.
Put the 700 g of the small bag on top of the thousands.
Write the grams in three places: 90 g has no hundreds.
Keep a 0 in the hundreds place after the thousands.
items.win: Yes, 2 kg 90 g is 2,090 g, with the 0 kept.

ladder: How many thousands are there in 4,000 g?
After the last full bag, is any rice left over?
items.win: Yes, 4,000 g is 4 kg 0 g, nothing left.

ladder: The thousands digit tells how many bags are full.
The three digits after the comma are the grams left.
After the comma come 0, 0 and then one more digit.
Zeros in front add nothing to a number of grams.
750 g and 600 g make 1,000 g and some more grams.
After the 1 kg is carried, how many grams are left over?
items.win: Yes, 5 kg 350 g: a kilogram was carried.

ladder: After borrowing, the top kilograms are one fewer.
Take 380 g from 1,140 g, then 2 kg from the top kilograms.
items.win: Yes, 2 kg 760 g of flour is left.

ladder: Count the kilograms too: 2 kg, 1 kg and the carried 1 kg.
The carry took exactly 1,000 g: what stays in the grams column?
items.win: Yes, 4 kg 0 g: all the grams became 1 kg.

ladder: Do 650 g and 140 g reach 1,000 g?
Add each column on its own: no carry is needed.
items.win: Yes, together they weigh 3 kg 790 g.

ladder: Add the grams of all three items: 1,000 g or more?
Every 1,000 g of the grams total is one more kilogram.
Can 600 g come out of 50 g, or must you borrow?
Borrow 1 kg as 1,000 g for the grams on top.
items.win: Yes, 2 kg 450 g is left in the bag.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, no colour means good or bad. The miss empties the answer slot at once (every digit, every box, a picked choice), so it is empty through the traceback; the pad re-opens empty after it.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The opened bags light one by one, counted in kilograms, then the small bag of grams; the total is left for the child.
Phase 2: The heap comes back whole and the 1 kg bags refill one by one, stopping one bag short: no count, no total, no Left ring.
Phase 3: The grams column lights first, the carry or the borrow shows again, then the kilograms column lights; the answer row stays empty.
Phase 4: The grams column lights first, a carry or a borrow is drawn, then the kilograms column lights; the answer row stays empty.

voice.opening: A scale and bags of rice: let us see what is inside a kilogram.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play: choose how many bags of rice, then tap Open to see the grams.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: You changed kilograms and grams both ways, and you worked the columns grams first.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

items.planQuestion: A bag of flour weighs 2 kg. How many grams is that?

question.en: The rice on the scale weighs 2 kg; how many grams is that?

items.planQuestion: A parcel weighs 4 kg 700 g. How many grams is that?

question.en: How many grams in all is 4 kg 700 g of rice?

items.planQuestion: A bag of oranges weighs 2 kg 90 g. How many grams is that?

question.en: This rice is 2 kg 90 g: write it in grams.

items.planAnswer: 2090 g, because 2 kg is two thousand grams and the 90 g goes after it with a zero kept, so the answer is 2090 g and not 290 g

question.en: This heap of rice weighs 4,000 g; how many kilograms and grams is that?
Now gather 3,450 g of rice: how many kg, and how many g are left over?
Gather 5,007 g of rice the same way: what is it in kg and g?
How much do 3 kg 750 g of rice and 1 kg 600 g of dal weigh in all?

items.planQuestion: A sack of flour weighs 5 kg 140 g. A baker uses 2 kg 380 g. How much flour is left?

question.en: From 5 kg 140 g of flour, a baker uses 2 kg 380 g; how much flour is left?

items.planAnswer: 2 kg 760 g, because 140 g is fewer than 380 g, so one kilogram is changed into one thousand grams, and 1140 g minus 380 g is 760 g and 4 kg minus 2 kg is 2 kg

question.en: Add 2 kg 600 g of sugar and 1 kg 400 g of flour: what is the total weight?

items.planQuestion: A basket holds 2 kg 650 g of apples and 1 kg 140 g of oranges. How much fruit is in the basket?

question.en: A 2 kg 650 g watermelon and 1 kg 140 g of mangoes: how much in all?
Find the total: 3 kg of rice, a 2 kg 500 g watermelon, 600 g of mangoes.
Take a 2 kg 600 g watermelon out of a 5 kg 50 g bag: how much is left?

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
